presentingComplaint: Oozing from IV cannula sites, bruising, and worsening confusion 3 days after admission for septic shock secondary to E. coli pyelonephritis.
history: 58-year-old woman admitted 3 days ago with fever, rigors and flank pain, diagnosed with E. coli pyelonephritis complicated by septic shock requiring vasopressor support. Over the last 24 hours the nursing staff note persistent ooze from venepuncture and arterial line sites, new bruising over the forearms, and gum bleeding on toothbrushing. Family report she has become increasingly drowsy and less responsive over the same period. No prior bleeding disorder, not on anticoagulants, no known liver disease. No history of recent trauma or surgery.
examination: Toxic-looking, drowsy but rousable to voice (GCS 13). Widespread petechiae and ecchymoses over the forearms and abdomen. Oozing blood from arterial line and peripheral IV sites that does not stop with pressure dressing. Mild gum bleeding. No focal neurological deficit. Abdomen soft, mild right flank tenderness. Extremities warm-to-cool with mottling, capillary refill 4 seconds. Chest clear. No overt gastrointestinal bleeding noted at this time.
imaging: CT abdomen/pelvis (prior to deterioration): right-sided perinephric stranding consistent with pyelonephritis, no abscess
CT head (non-contrast, for altered sensorium): no acute hemorrhage or mass lesion
microbiology: Blood cultures (drawn on admission): E. coli, pan-sensitive, growing in 2/2 bottles
Urine culture: E. coli >10^5 CFU/mL, concordant sensitivities
differentialDiagnoses: Disseminated intravascular coagulation secondary to sepsis
Dilutional coagulopathy from massive fluid resuscitation
citations: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Sepsis and Septic Shock
International Society on Thrombosis and Haemostasis (ISTH) DIC Scoring Guidance 2001/2018
stewardship: Continue source-directed empirical antimicrobials for the underlying E. coli urosepsis (e.g., a broad-spectrum beta-lactam such as piperacillin-tazobactam or a third-generation cephalosporin, de-escalated per culture sensitivities) per Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021; DIC management itself is supportive (treat the underlying trigger, transfuse blood products as indicated for active bleeding) rather than antimicrobial-specific.
contraindications: Avoid antifibrinolytics (e.g., tranexamic acid) in DIC with a dominant bleeding phenotype unless hyperfibrinolysis is clearly documented, as they may worsen microvascular thrombosis
Avoid unfractionated/low-molecular-weight heparin in the actively bleeding phase of DIC
Avoid delaying source control/antimicrobials while correcting coagulopathy - treating the underlying sepsis is the priority intervention
edgeCases: Distinguishing DIC from TTP/HUS is critical: DIC has prolonged PT/aPTT and low fibrinogen, whereas TTP/HUS typically has normal coagulation parameters with prominent schistocytosis and severe thrombocytopenia - this case has both prolonged PT/aPTT and low fibrinogen with high D-dimer, favoring DIC
Chronic/compensated DIC can present with a thrombotic rather than bleeding phenotype; this case represents the acute decompensated bleeding phenotype typical of sepsis-associated DIC
Liver dysfunction from shock/hypoperfusion can independently prolong INR and lower fibrinogen, confounding the DIC score - clinical correlation with ISTH scoring is required
DIC itself is a laboratory/clinical syndrome overlying the underlying sepsis; the disease list used by the engine represents the closest coded entity (dic) for this presentation
expectedMaiK: MaiK should flag decompensated DIC (ISTH overt score consistent) in the context of septic shock - recommend treating the underlying sepsis, transfusing platelets/FFP/cryoprecipitate for active bleeding, avoiding antifibrinolytics, and closely monitoring for progression to multiorgan failure.
expectedNextQuestions: Is there any history of liver disease, anticoagulant use, or a pre-existing bleeding disorder?
Are there signs of active major hemorrhage (GI bleed, intracranial bleed) requiring urgent blood product transfusion?
What is the trend in platelet count, fibrinogen, and D-dimer over the last 24-48 hours?
Has source control been achieved for the underlying urosepsis (repeat imaging, catheter/stent if obstruction present)?
Is the patient a transfusion candidate, and are blood products (platelets, FFP, cryoprecipitate) available?
